10. Management, incentives and capital allocation

The team

Officer Role In seat since Prior record
Nikesh Arora Chairman and CEO June 2018 President and COO of SoftBank; earlier Chief Business Officer at Google
Dipak Golechha EVP, CFO May 2021 Finance roles outside cybersecurity; the third CFO under Arora
William "BJ" Jenkins President August 2022 CEO of Barracuda Networks
Lee Klarich EVP, Chief Product and Technology Officer 2017 as CPO; product-and-technology title from fiscal 2024 Joined PANW in 2006; took the CTO remit from Nir Zuk
Nir Zuk Founder Emeritus Founder 2005; ceased to be an executive officer 2025-08-14 Founder and long-time CTO

The CFO seat turned over three times in three years before Golechha, and the President seat twice. Eleven directors served at the 2025 proxy; Arora is both Chairman and CEO, and John M. Donovan is Lead Independent Director and serves on the Compensation and People Committee. Carl Eschenbach has been a director since May 2013 and has been CEO of Workday since December 2022; Workday is one of the sixteen companies in PANW's fiscal 2025 compensation peer group, and Eschenbach serves on the Security Committee.

Compensation design

The annual cash incentive is based on two corporate measures, revenue and organic non-GAAP operating margin, the latter defined as excluding "the effects of acquisitions and dispositions." For fiscal 2025 the revenue target was $9,112m against $9,222m delivered and the margin target 27.8% against 29.1%, producing a 120% payout with no committee discretion applied. The $9,112m target equals the low end of the fiscal 2025 revenue guidance published in November 2024.

All fiscal 2025 executive equity was performance-based. The design changed that year and again for fiscal 2026: the maximum payout was cut by a third, from 600% to 400% of target, including for already-outstanding awards; the financial measures became NGS ARR and non-GAAP diluted EPS, equally weighted, applied to the remaining performance periods of the fiscal 2023 and fiscal 2024 awards as well as to new grants; and a relative total-shareholder-return modifier against the S&P 500 applies on top. For fiscal 2026 the 1.0x modifier now requires the 55th percentile instead of the 50th, and the 300% maximum on the NGS ARR measure requires beating target by at least $400m.

The structure has not paid near its maximum. The fiscal 2022 awards reached about 51% of a 300% maximum despite a 98th-percentile total-shareholder-return rank; the fiscal 2023 awards about 68% at a 93rd-percentile rank. Arora's fiscal 2023 retention award, reported at $113,550,000, has a five-year cliff, pays nothing below the 40th percentile of the S&P 500 and requires continuous employment throughout.

The measures are asymmetric on acquisitions in a way the proxy states plainly. The cash-bonus margin measure excludes acquisitions by definition. The long-term equity measure does not: "the scope of products, subscriptions, and support offerings that contribute to NGS ARR will generally increase over time as we introduce or acquire new next-generation products." An acquisition adds to the equity measure by construction while its dilution to operating margin is stripped out of the annual bonus. The size of that is disclosed: $1.63bn of the $8.13bn NGS ARR at 2026-04-30, 20%, came from CyberArk and Chronosphere. Two features run the other way and belong beside it: non-GAAP EPS became an equally weighted equity measure from fiscal 2025 and is diluted by the 112m shares issued for CyberArk, and ownership guidelines exclude unvested units and unexercised options with a one-year post-vesting hold on all named executives.

Realised pay, ownership and the shareholder vote

Fiscal 2025 realised value across the five named executives was $1,406,612,074, of which roughly $1.24bn came from option exercises — the performance-based options granted in fiscal 2018 and fiscal 2019 reaching their stock-price targets. Arora realised $658.8m, Zuk $492.1m and Klarich $215.4m. Over the same two years their split-adjusted beneficial ownership declined 61%, 51% and 63% respectively. Beneficial ownership counts shares issuable within 60 days, so part of each change reflects what was exercisable at the measurement date; no local Form 4 record covers PANW to separate open-market activity from derivative settlement. All directors and executive officers as a group held 1.4% of shares outstanding at 2025-09-15; Vanguard held 8.2% and BlackRock 7.3%. The CEO pay ratio was 442:1 for fiscal 2025, measured against a median employee identified for fiscal 2023 and reused in both fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2025, so the denominator is a three-year-old employee profile against a headcount that has gone from 16,068 to 21,491.

Say-on-pay failed twice in three years: 38% support for fiscal 2023 pay, "a majority" for fiscal 2024 with no percentage disclosed, and 46.6% for fiscal 2025 (221,211,579 for against 253,792,757 opposed). The programme that failed in December 2025 was the redesigned one. At the same meeting holders approved 10 million more shares for the equity plan by 95.2%, rejected a shareholder proposal to exclude buyback effects from incentive metrics at 3.1% support, and approved annual election of all directors at 93.8% against the board's recommendation. Donovan drew 100.8m votes against, four times the opposition to the other two nominees.

Candor

Billings was the headline top-line metric on every call from fiscal 2016 through fiscal 2024 and has not been spoken on a call since Q4 FY2025. Mentions per call went 33, 22, 27, 24 across FY2024, then 5, 1, 1, 2 across FY2025 and zero in every quarter of FY2026. Golechha announced the removal on the Q1 FY2025 call: "The quarterly analysis of billings is no longer meaningful as it does not reflect how we now run the business." NGS ARR then became the proxy's company-selected measure and a financial measure in the fiscal 2025 equity awards. The same pattern is now one level up: the organic-versus-acquired breakout was given at the two quarters where organic growth became the contested question and is being withdrawn at the third.

Across eleven years of earnings calls, from Q4 FY2016 to Q3 FY2026, the concession vocabulary is narrow. "In hindsight" is used twice, both times by McLaughlin in fiscal 2017; "disappointed" three times, in fiscal 2017 and fiscal 2020; "we should have" three times; and "we underestimated," "we were wrong" and "took longer than" never. Under Arora the concession vocabulary is close to absent across roughly thirty calls, including the quarter of the largest guidance reduction in the company's history, which he presented as a chosen strategy: "Our guidance is not a consequence of a change in the demand outlook out there. Our guidance is a consequence of us driving a shift in our strategy."

Buybacks absorbed 31.3% of cumulative free cash flow over the decade, acquisition cash 27.6% and convertible repayment 26.1%; capital expenditure took 8.7% of operating cash flow. Nine months of fiscal 2026 spent more acquisition cash, $4,563m, than the whole preceding decade, and adding the stock, total FY2026 purchase consideration for Chronosphere, CyberArk and Koi is $24,243m, roughly 5.4x the prior decade's cash outlay.

Repurchases track cash generation and authorisation headroom, not price. In FY2017-FY2021 free cash flow totalled $4,764m and repurchases $3,376m, 70.9% of it. In FY2022-FY2025 free cash flow totalled $10,994m and repurchases $1,732m, 15.8%. The two largest free cash flow years in the company's history, FY2025 at $3,470m and FY2024 at $3,101m, produced the joint-lowest and the fourth-lowest repurchase ratios of the decade at 0% and 18.3%. The word "opportunistic" appears in the buyback sentence on nearly every call from FY2021 through FY2026, including the six consecutive quarters in which nothing was bought. The February 2026 tranche is the exception and the best-timed of the decade: 6.8m shares at $147.69 for $1,000m, worth $2,527m at the 2026-08-28 close, bought against an authorisation the board had to top up by $1.0bn three weeks later. The worst is the Q2 FY2022 tranche at about $534 as filed, $89 on the current split basis, paid within weeks of the pre-split peak.

The employee-equity offset. PANW expensed $7,941m of share-based compensation over FY2016-FY2025, 17.4% of cumulative revenue, against $5,108m of repurchase, an offset of 0.64x. The split-adjusted basic share count rose 26.8% over nine years while repurchases retired 120.4m shares against gross issuance near 260m. The only year the average count declined was FY2021, after the two largest repurchase years back to back.

11. M&A, divestitures and deal track record

Through fiscal 2025 PANW was a disciplined serial acquirer. The security-operations and endpoint deals — Cyvera, LightCyber, Secdo, Demisto, Expanse, Crypsis, the IBM QRadar assets and Koi — cost $3,236m in total and underpin a Cortex platform that passed $1bn of ARR in fiscal Q1 2026 and an XSIAM line above $600m growing 100%. The three SASE deals cost $888m against SASE ARR of $1.6bn growing 40%. Both books cost less than one year of the ARR they now support, nothing has been impaired, nothing has been divested, and no acquired business has been reported as a discontinued operation.

Two facts qualify that. Sixty-nine per cent of everything PANW has ever spent on acquisitions went into a single transaction that closed 2.6 months before the last reported balance-sheet date, so the largest deal has almost no outcome evidence attached to it. And the one transaction with a contractual outcome test written into it, the IBM QRadar earn-out, has been marked down twice and renegotiated once, which is the only quantified signal that an acquired asset is converting more slowly than PANW underwrote.

PANW amended the terms with IBM in June 2025 and cut the estimated undiscounted range of remaining payments from $0.4-0.6bn to $0.3-0.5bn. Cumulative fair-value reductions are $255m, 39% of the amount booked at close, attributed to "the magnitude and likelihood of customers entering into qualified new transactions, the competitive industry environment, and current market conditions." Two consequences follow. The economic price is trending toward roughly $500m of cash plus $390m of contingent payments against the $1,143m booked, so the deal gets cheaper as it underdelivers against its own schedule. And the mark-downs run through general and administrative expense as gains — $135.3m in fiscal 2025 and $120m across nine months of fiscal 2026, including $110m in Q3 alone, which is 35% of the $316m of general and administrative expense PANW reported that quarter. The strategic purpose worked: XSIAM bookings went from over $200m in fiscal 2023 to roughly $500m in fiscal 2024 and past $1bn cumulative by fiscal Q2 2025, and management sized the QRadar migration pipeline at $1bn of total value.

Weighted-average cost of debt: 0.0%, on both a principal-weighted coupon basis and a cash-interest basis. Interest expense for the nine months ended 2026-04-30 was zero. The last cash coupon PANW paid was on the 0.375% 2025 Notes, which matured 2025-06-01.

PANW has never issued a straight corporate bond. Every dollar of borrowed money since the IPO has been a zero- or near-zero-coupon convertible: $575m of 0.00% notes due 2019, $1,693m of 0.75% notes due 2023, $2,000m of 0.375% notes due 2025, and now the assumed $1,250m of 0.00% notes due 2030. At 2025-07-31 PANW had no debt on the balance sheet for the first time since fiscal 2014; the 2030 Notes came back onto it through the CyberArk close, not through a financing decision.

Each $1,000 of 2030 Notes is exchangeable for approximately 4.3161 PANW shares plus $88.2630 of cash, an effective conversion price near $211.24, and PANW pays the principal in cash and settles the excess in cash, stock or a combination at its own election. Holders may convert during a calendar quarter if the stock closed at or above $280.75 on at least 20 of the 30 trading days ending the prior quarter; 13 of 30 closes met that in the window ending 2026-06-30 and 30 of 30 in the window ending 2026-08-28, so at prices near current levels the notes become convertible from 2026-10-01 and about $1.1bn of principal reclassifies to a current liability at the 2026-10-31 balance-sheet date. And PANW may call them at par from 2028-06-20 on the same price condition.

At the 2026-08-28 close of $371.59, 75.9% above the conversion price, conversion value on the remaining $1,097m is about $1,858m: 4.7m shares worth $1,761m plus $97m of cash. Less the $1,097m of principal payable in cash, the excess is $761m, against which the assumed capped calls cover about $370m at their $287.21-$291.44 cap, leaving roughly $391m uncovered [estimate: pro-rating the disclosed $1,250m-principal exchange terms to the $1,097m remaining and valuing the share leg at the 2026-08-28 close; the capped-call offset ranges $360m-$380m across the two disclosed cap prices, so the uncovered figure ranges $381m-$401m]. Above roughly $289 the capped calls stop offsetting, and every dollar of share price above that level is uncovered.

PANW elected the fair value option on these notes, so changes in their value run through other income and move with PANW's own share price. Marking them from the disclosed 2026-04-30 fair value of $1,192m to conversion value at the 2026-07-31 close of $331.83, and the capped calls from their disclosed $94m to intrinsic value, a non-cash charge of roughly $200m-$270m is already determined for the fiscal fourth quarter [estimate: conversion value at 2026-07-31 of about $1,669m gives a mark-to-market loss of $477m as a minimum and roughly $540m allowing for time value, against a capped-call gain near $276m]. None of it is cash and none of it is an operating result.

Peak leverage was fiscal 2020, when $3,693m of convertibles stood against $1,036m of operating cash flow. That resolved without action: the notes converted into stock or were repaid out of a cash flow line that more than tripled by fiscal 2025. PANW had no covenant breach, no rating action and no forced refinancing. Liquidity declined $1,468m across nine months of fiscal 2026 despite $3,196m of operating cash flow, because $4,563m went out for acquisitions, $1,000m for buybacks, $154m for contingent consideration and $125m for tax withholding on equity settlements. A 100 basis point rise in rates would reduce the fair value of the investment portfolio by $96m, realised only on a pre-maturity sale.

Customers fund the balance sheet. Deferred revenue at 2026-04-30 was $13,605m, split $7,113m current and $6,492m long-term, against total liabilities of $18,598m. Customer prepayments are 73.2% of everything PANW owes and they cost nothing. PANW lends some of it back: net financing receivables were $1,370m, down from $1,717m at 2025-07-31, and new originations are running about 37% below fiscal 2025 annualised. Net customer float is therefore $12,235m. Credit quality on the internal scale is roughly stable — buckets 5 to 10 were 27.5% of the book against 27.1% — though the worst bucket grew from $18m to $38m, or from 1.0% to 2.7%.

Structural balance-sheet risks, ranked by the size of the obligation at risk

  1. Cloud purchase commitments, $8,092m through fiscal 2031 and beyond. Non-cancelable, growing 23.0% in nine months, back-loaded after a 42% cut to the fiscal 2027 tranche, and seven times the size of the debt.
  2. Share-based compensation re-inflating. 22.8% of revenue in Q3 FY2026, 16.9% excluding acquisition acceleration, against 13.4% in fiscal 2024, with $3.6bn unvested amortising over 2.6 years before new grants.
  3. The 2030 Notes conversion, roughly $391m uncovered at the current share price, with reclassification to a current liability likely at the 2026-10-31 balance-sheet date on current prices.
  4. Earnings volatility from the fair value election. Other income now moves with PANW's own share price, and a charge of roughly $200m-$270m for fiscal Q4 2026 is already determined by the 2026-07-31 close.
  5. Goodwill and intangibles above book equity. $29,185m against $27,668m, tested as a single reporting unit until segment reporting begins.
  6. Contingent consideration, $240m, split $124m current and $116m long-term after $154m of payments and a $120m fair-value gain across nine months.
  7. The Centripetal judgment, $150m accrued, covered by a surety bond pending appeal.
  8. Refinancing and floating-rate exposure, neither material. One maturity in June 2030, an undrawn revolver, one borrower, unsecured, no subsidiary debt.
  9. Jurisdiction. Israeli long-lived assets were $162.1m at 2025-07-31, 22.1% of the total and second only to the United States, and CyberArk is an Israeli company, so a larger share of the cost base is now outside the dollar. PANW hedges with forward contracts, a $5m net liability at 2026-04-30, and gives no notional.

What drove value across the decade

Revenue compounded 23.5% a year from FY2016 to FY2025 and the composition changed completely. Subscription revenue compounded 34.0% and went from 25.9% of revenue to 53.9%; support compounded 24.1%; product compounded 11.6% and went from 48.7% of revenue to 19.5%. The geographic mix barely moved: the United States went from 65.4% to 62.7% and EMEA from 17.9% to 20.8%.

Operating margin moved in four steps.

Fiscal year Δ gross margin Δ R&D leverage Δ S&M leverage Δ G&A leverage Δ operating margin Operating margin

FY2021 (0.6) (4.3) +3.4 (0.4) (1.9) (7.1)%
FY2022 (1.3) +1.0 +2.1 +1.8 +3.7 (3.4)%
FY2023 +3.5 +2.5 +2.2 +0.9 +9.1 5.6%
FY2024 +2.1 +0.7 +2.1 (2.0) +2.9 8.5%
FY2025 (0.9) +1.0 +1.2 +3.7 +5.0 13.5%

FY2020 and FY2021 are the Cortex and cloud-security build: research and development went from 18.6% of revenue in FY2019 to 26.8% in FY2021, an absolute increase of $600.9m in two years, while gross margin declined 210 basis points as the cloud-hosted subscription mix grew. FY2023 recovered 350 basis points of gross margin on higher software mix and support-cost scale and levered every operating-expense line. FY2024 expanded 290 basis points despite a 200-basis-point general and administrative drag from $204.4m of litigation charges. FY2025 expanded 500 basis points of which 370 came from general and administrative, and three named items account for $378.5m of that, 4.1 points of revenue: the FY2024 litigation charges did not repeat, PANW released $38.8m of litigation accrual, and it booked a $135.3m gain on the change in fair value of the IBM QRadar contingent consideration. Four-fifths of the FY2025 GAAP operating-margin expansion came from items that will not repeat in the same form.▪

Across FY2020 to FY2025 the 18.8 points of GAAP operating-margin expansion split as +2.7 from gross margin, +1.0 from research and development, +11.1 from sales and marketing and +4.0 from general and administrative.▪ Sales and marketing supplied nearly 60% of it, declining from 44.7% of revenue to 33.6% while revenue tripled. The installed-base annuity is why: renewals and attach expansions on a million deployed appliances cost far less to sell than the original land. Share-based compensation declined from 19.3% of revenue to 14.0% over the same five years, which accounts for about five of the eighteen points; the remaining thirteen are cash leverage.

Cash conversion runs far ahead of accounting profit. FY2025 free cash flow of $3,469.8m was 37.6% of revenue against a 13.5% GAAP operating margin, and the difference is $1,295.1m of share-based compensation, $343.4m of depreciation and amortisation, and growth in deferred revenue.▪ Days sales outstanding on receivables alone doubled from 73 days in FY2019 to 142 in FY2022 and came back to 98 on trailing revenue at 2026-04-30; adding the deferred-payment financing receivables, the peak was 206 days in FY2024 and the level is now 145. That 60-day improvement is worth roughly $1.75bn of working capital on FY2026 trailing revenue and is a large part of why free cash flow has held up.

Billings, the metric that was withdrawn. PANW published billings as a headline metric from FY2014 through FY2024 and guided to it every quarter. Growth went 37.0% (FY2022), 23.1% (FY2023), 11.0% (FY2024) and roughly 3% in FY2025 on PANW's own formula [estimate: revenue plus the change in total deferred revenue, the company's definition, applied to FY2025 balances of $12,751.9m and $11,480.5m and revenue of $9,221.5m gives $10,492.9m and +2.8%; acquired deferred revenue from Protect AI and the QRadar assets is not disclosed for FY2025, so 2.8% is the maximum and the range is 2.0%-2.8%]. The metric left the outlook on 2024-08-19 and the FY2025 10-K does not report it. The mechanical explanation management gave is real: the mix shifted toward annual billing on multi-year contracts and away from PANW-originated financing, both of which reduce cash invoiced up front without touching the contract, and two disclosed series confirm the contract base kept growing — remaining performance obligations rose 24.4% in FY2025 and NGS ARR 32%. The bridge management supplied, that FY2025 billings would have grown 12% on unchanged practices, has no realised counterpart because billings was never reported again.

Three KPIs inflected. XSIAM's average ARR per customer broke a multi-quarter trend, moving below $1m for the first time since the metric was published, with customer count growing faster than ARR in each of the last two disclosed quarters. Observability went from nothing to above $300m in two quarters through acquisition plus one customer's consumption. And the hardware line reversed a four-year stall in a single quarter, with a price increase, a generation change and an industry refresh all landing at once.

The gross-margin drop landed entirely in the CyberArk quarter — 74.2% in Q1 FY2026 and 73.6% in Q2, then 67.6% — as amortisation of acquired intangibles rose to $280m from $43m a year earlier and purchase accounting wrote CyberArk's deferred revenue down to $776m, suppressing acquired revenue while leaving the cost of delivering it. GAAP operating income went from +$218.8m to −$183.0m, and the 10-Q gives the split: the two acquisitions contributed $388m of revenue and a $523m operating loss, so the rest of PANW earned about $340m on about $2,614m of organic revenue, a 13.0% GAAP operating margin against 9.6% a year earlier. Non-GAAP operating margin of 27.1% is 320 basis points below the immediately preceding quarter and 30 below the year-ago quarter, and the FY2026 guide of 28.9-29.2% would be the smallest annual increase since FY2022. And nine-month capital expenditure of $337m against $159.9m a year earlier includes the $91m land purchase; excluding it, nine-month capex is about 3.0% of revenue against 2.7% for FY2025.

Four things confirm the FY2025 pattern: organic revenue growth at 14-16% for seven straight quarters, the free cash flow level, the net cash position, and the operating cash flow seasonality.

14. Expectations: internal, external and base rates

Management and the street are within a rounding of each other on the top line, and they differ on how much of it becomes cash: consensus takes the free cash flow margin from 37.6% in FY2025 to 40.9% by FY2029, and PANW's own adjusted margin has gone 38.8%, 38.9%, 38.0% and a guided 37.5% across FY2023 to FY2026.

Driver Internal (management) External (consensus) Where and why they disagree Base rate
Total revenue FY2026 guided $11.415-11.425bn, +24% reported. Medium-term target of 17-19% a year to FY2026, set August 2023 FY2026E $11,421m, FY2027E $13,837m (+21.2%), FY2028E $15,747m (+13.8%), FY2029E $17,762m; 17.8% a year for four years No disagreement on FY2026: consensus is at the guidance midpoint on 44 estimates with a standard deviation of 0.05%. On FY2027 the gap is the base: on the 10-Q's own pro forma FY2026 of about $12,267m, consensus FY2027 is +12.8% against a combined group growing 16-17% now 17.8% is the 59th percentile of software issuers at $7-13bn growing above 12% and the 88th of security and infrastructure issuers above $3bn; the median four-year forward CAGR is 14.4% and 11.6% respectively
Organic revenue Organic growth of 14.2% in Q3 FY2026, 14.9% over nine months, disclosed twice and being withdrawn No organic line exists in the consensus set Consensus has no organic estimate to disagree with. Stripping the acquisitions, consensus for the legacy business implies about 11.7% a year to FY2029 [estimate: acquired revenue of $1.75bn annualised at 2026-04-30 compounded at 20-35% to the FY2029 midpoint, giving $2.9-4.0bn] About 11.7% is the 29th percentile of the scale-matched class and the 53rd of the industry-matched class, so the legacy ask is at or slightly below the median software company of this size and growth

FY2026 consensus is a copy of guidance: revenue of $11,421m is inside the guided $11.415-11.425bn, EPS of $3.777 at the midpoint of $3.77-3.79, the implied 765m share count inside the guided 763-766m. The disagreement is about earnings, not revenue — in FY2028 the revenue spread across contributors is 15.7% of the mean and the EPS spread is 37.5%, and the FY2028 operating income range of $4,443m to $6,332m is a twelve-point margin disagreement against a sixteen-point revenue disagreement. And beyond FY2028 the contributor set thins from 38 to ten, six and five, so the outer years are not drawn from the same models: FY2029 revenue estimates run from $13,680m to $20,231m, and the low is below the FY2028 mean.

Estimate revisions ran against the price. Over the twelve months to 2026-07-31 the stock rose 91%, and to 2026-08-28 it rose 95%. Over the same twelve months FY2027 consensus EPS was cut 4.1%, FY2026 1.0% and FY2028 0.9%. The revenue lines rose, but 7 to 14 points of each rise is the February consolidation of two acquired businesses; excluding that step, twelve-month revenue revisions are +1.3% for FY2026, +2.4% for FY2027 and +2.8% for FY2028. Across the fourteen-name cohort only Check Point shares the negative earnings revision, and its stock declined 28%.

Ratings and targets disagree with each other. Of the 57 recommendations set or reaffirmed since the 2026-06-02 print, 44 are buy-equivalent, 77%, and the consensus rating of 4.54 on Bloomberg's 1-to-5 scale is near the top of its range. Bloomberg's published target of $369.39 is 0.6% below the last close, and 25 of the 50 targets set since the print sit below it. Firms that updated in August raised sharply — Wells Fargo $475, Truist $435, RBC $434, Cantor $425, Needham $425 — while the cluster set in the two days after the print runs $201 to $350. Two positions pair a positive rating with a target well below spot: Bernstein reaffirmed outperform on 2026-08-27 at $253, and Scotiabank sector outperform on 2026-08-26 at $320. The bear positions reach their targets by applying a historically ordinary multiple to a roughly consensus earnings number: HSBC's $201 is 52.9x the lowest published FY2027 EPS estimate and Roth's $210 is 55.3x, both inside the 36.2x-56.0x band the stock's average forward multiple held from FY2017 through FY2025.

PANW's own base rates

The one completed multi-year cycle was met. At the September 2021 Analyst Day PANW set FY2024 targets of $8.0bn of revenue, $10.0bn of billings and $3.25bn of NGS ARR; it delivered $8,027.5m, about $10.2bn and $4.22bn. The cycle now closing is the August 2023 medium-term plan, and it splits by basis.

FY2026 target set 2023-08-18 On the reported basis On the organic basis
Revenue growth 17-19% a year from $6,892.7m $11,420m = 18.3% a year, met ~$10,550m = 15.3% a year, missed
RPO growth 25% a year from $10.6bn $20.95bn = 25.5% a year, met ~$18.9bn = 21.2% a year, missed
Non-GAAP operating margin 28-29% guided 28.9-29.2%, met —
Non-GAAP EPS compounding above 20% from $2.22 $3.78 = 19.4% a year, missed by 0.6 of a point —
NGS ARR above 55% of FY2026 revenue $8.925bn / $11.42bn = 78%, beaten $6.5bn / $10.55bn = 62%, beaten

Two of the five scoreable targets were met only because CyberArk and Chronosphere arrived inside the target window.▪ The one the acquisitions could not help, non-GAAP EPS, is missed on the company's own guidance, because issuing 112 million shares dilutes the denominator the same acquisition inflates the numerator through.

On the quarterly record the guide is set to be beaten and the cushion has narrowed. Across 23 guided quarters from Q1 FY2021 to Q3 FY2026, revenue finished above the guided high end 18 times, inside the range 5 times and below the low end never; non-GAAP EPS finished above the high end all 23 times. The mean revenue beat against the guided midpoint was +2.82% in FY2021-FY2022, +0.94% in FY2023-FY2024 and +1.04% in FY2025-FY2026. The two narrowest revenue beats in the whole record are the two most recent standalone quarters, each exactly $4m above the guided high end. Against consensus, PANW beat non-GAAP EPS in 18 of the 19 quarters from Q1 FY2022, with a median beat of +6.8%, an FY2023 average of +22.0% and a last-eight-quarter median of +6.1%. Consensus now sits within 1% of the guidance midpoint on revenue in every recent quarter, so a beat measures how much conservatism management builds into a guide.

The Q4 FY2026 margin step the guide requires

Non-GAAP operating margin by quarter in FY2026 was 30.2%, 30.3% and 27.1%. Nine-month revenue was $8,070m and the Q4 guide is $3.345-3.355bn. Holding Q1 and Q2 at their reported $746m and $785m, nine-month non-GAAP operating income is $2,345m; the full-year guide of 28.9-29.2% on $11.42bn implies $3,300-3,335m, leaving $955-990m for Q4, or 28.5-29.6% [estimate: full-year guided margin less the computed nine-month result]. Q4 FY2026 therefore needs 140 to 250 basis points of sequential margin improvement in the first quarter that includes a full period of CyberArk, plus Portkey from 2026-05-29, against a Q3 that included only 2.6 months of CyberArk and still gave up roughly 300 basis points sequentially.▪ Management's stated support is CyberArk synergies arriving three to six months early, more than 300 IT vendors identified for streamlining with about 20% actioned, improved cloud hosting economics for the acquired business, and over 40 acquired facilities under review. It resolves on 2026-09-01.

GAAP EPS was negative in every year through FY2022, so the trailing multiple is on the non-GAAP basis throughout to keep it comparable; on GAAP it is undefined before FY2023, then 195x, 45x and 109x. FY2024 GAAP EPS of $3.64 is not an operating result — it includes the deferred-tax valuation-allowance release, which lifted fiscal Q2 2024 GAAP diluted EPS to $2.45 against $0.73 non-GAAP for the same quarter. The perfect-foresight column divides each fiscal-year-end price by the following year's realised non-GAAP EPS and uses hindsight; it is shown to separate what the market paid from what it got. EV/EBITDA is on GAAP EBITDA, which is after share-based compensation, so it is marked n/m where EBITDA was negative or near zero and becomes informative only from FY2023. Price to book has never been the basis this stock traded on: book value per share went from $1.31 at FY2021 to $0.35 at FY2022 as buybacks and convertible settlements eroded common equity, putting the FY2022 year-end multiple at 237x, then rebuilt to $11.71 by FY2025 and, after the CyberArk share issuance, to $34.03 at 2026-08-28 for a current multiple of 10.9x.

The deepest decline was the 48.0% fall from February 2019 to the COVID low; the longest was the 45.2% fall from July 2015 to April 2017, which came with the two large sales-execution misses of FY2017 and took until May 2018 to recover. The 2024 drawdown is the outlier for speed, losing 30.5% in seven trading sessions around the platformization guidance cut.

Largest single-session moves of the decade: −28.4% on 2024-02-21, −24.2% on 2017-03-01 (the fiscal Q2 2017 miss), +18.6% on 2021-08-24, +17.2% on 2017-06-01, −17.0% on 2020-02-25, +14.8% on 2023-08-21, +13.4% on 2025-04-09 (a market-wide session) and +12.8% on 2026-08-27.

The most recent rally is the largest of the decade: from the 2026-02-24 low of $141.67 to the 2026-08-13 high of $396.00 the stock rose 179% in under six months. Three dated events fall inside it. On 2026-05-07 the shares rose 7.0% after Fortinet reported the prior evening and PANW, Zscaler and CrowdStrike all rose together (markets.financialcontent.com, accessed 2026-08-29) [web]. May 2026 as a whole added 57.1%, spanning the Idira launch on 2026-05-12 and the Portkey close on 2026-05-29 (finance.yahoo.com, accessed 2026-08-29) [web]. And on 2026-08-27 the shares rose 12.8% after a report that the company was examining Cribl and ClickHouse as acquisition targets, and that earlier approaches to Okta and Datadog had failed (fool.com, accessed 2026-08-29) [web]. The company has not confirmed that report. The move gave back 2.9% the following session.

Measured on the full-year-ownership base of $12,267m so that the CyberArk and Chronosphere annualisation does not inflate it, base revenue compounds 13.6% from FY2026 to FY2030 and 11.0% to FY2035; bear 6.9% and 5.6%; bull 20.9% and 14.9%. The base sits just under the 14.4% median four-year forward CAGR of software issuers at $7-13bn of revenue and at the 60th percentile of security and infrastructure issuers. The bull is above the 90th percentile of both, and no completed episode in the 104-company reference class compounded at 15% for nine years from this scale.

The base grows slightly faster than consensus and converts less of it to cash: base revenue runs 2.7-3.3% above consensus across FY2027-FY2030 while base free cash flow runs 5.4% below in FY2028 and 11.0% below in FY2029, and the whole of that gap is the customer float. In the bear case nine years of revenue growth produce no earnings growth per share: revenue reaches $19,963m by FY2035, up 75% from FY2026, and free cash flow per share declines every year of the forecast. And Network Security is 75% of revenue today and 59% by FY2035 in the base case, with Cortex at 26% and Identity at 15%.▪ That is a $4.9bn installed-base annuity growing 4-7% a year alongside three books growing 12-47%.

The share count moves the per-share answer by more than any operating driver: one percentage point a year is worth $1.09 of FY2035 free cash flow per share, nearly double the largest revenue driver, it compounds over nine years and it requires no customer. Lower share-based compensation reduces free cash flow slightly, by $75m, because the charge is non-cash and removing a point of it raises taxable operating income; its real cost is the dilution the share-count row captures.

Four of those do not survive their own evidence.

Repurchases at 55% of free cash flow. PANW has never sustained that rate. Repurchases absorbed 31.3% of cumulative FY2016-FY2025 free cash flow, and the last five observations are 49.8%, 10.4%, 18.3%, 0% and 35.0% for nine months of FY2026, an average of 22.7%. The two largest free cash flow years in the company's history produced the joint-lowest and the fourth-lowest ratios of the decade. Management's framework ranks acquisitions first and calls buybacks opportunistic, and $1.0bn of authorisation remained at 2026-04-30 against a 2026-12-31 expiry. The evidence supports a base near 30-35% with a 0-70% range, and the assumption also runs against the share-count assumption in direction.

No further acquisitions. PANW has closed six since August 2024 for about $26.2bn of consideration; acquisition cash absorbed 54% of operating cash flow across FY2018-FY2021 and 143% of it across nine months of FY2026; over FY2016-FY2025 it was 27.6% of cumulative free cash flow, the second-largest use after repurchase, with no four-year window in company history free of a deal. Reporting on 2026-08-27 named Cribl at roughly $3.5bn and ClickHouse at roughly $15bn as current pursuits, and the shares rose 12.83% the day it appeared, which makes further deals more likely. The base case also reaches $17,148m of NGS ARR in fiscal 2030 against a $20bn target, a $2.9bn gap roughly the size of one CyberArk-scale identity book. The evidence supports at minimum $1-2bn a year of consideration and a material probability of one deal above $3bn inside the window; revenue, acquired-intangible amortisation, share count and goodwill would all be understated together.

SASE revenue per seat rising 4.2% a year. The bear (4.3%) exceeds the base (4.2%), so the total spread across all three scenarios is 0.2 of a percentage point on a series built from one deal. The direction also runs against the company's own contemporaneous evidence: average ARR per XSIAM customer declined about 25% in a year while the customer count grew about 175%, which is the same company expanding volume by cutting the average land. Prisma Access Browser licences quadrupled to 11 million with no separate price, and platformization converts per-module pricing into discounted committed spend. The evidence supports about −3% to +4% a year, centred near flat, and a flat price path takes base SASE ARR growth from 21.8% to 17.6%.

Certificate renewals at 3.65 per certificate in fiscal 2027. The CA/Browser Forum cut to 100 days takes effect on 2027-03-15, and PANW's fiscal 2027 runs 2026-08-01 to 2027-07-31, so 7.5 of 12 months fall under the 200-day regime at 1.83 renewals and only 4.5 months under the 100-day regime at 3.65; certificates issued before the step keep their existing lifetimes, lagging the effective rate by up to one full certificate life. The exposure-weighted fiscal 2027 figure is about 2.5. Separately, CyberArk's own 20-F states that machine identity is licensed per machine and credential, so more frequent renewals raise the necessity of automation without mechanically raising price or units. No revenue line in the model is keyed to this schedule.

A further set of assumptions is loosely identified, and the largest of them is the largest revenue line. The attached subscription and support block is a residual after product, SASE, Cortex and identity are removed from total revenue, its FY2026 anchor of about 7% growth is a difference of estimates, and neither of its components is well identified: the installed-base path implies a 5.1-year replacement life where the disclosed range runs to seven years, which at the long end would grow the base 8.7% a year instead of 3.0%, and the revenue-per-device series cannot be reconciled to support revenue at the published price ratios. The 2.1% to 9.8% range around it is the second-widest of any driver, and it brackets both disclosed anchors that touch the block. Two more are worth stating plainly: hardware units are measured off a peak quarter and the bear of −2% a year never contemplates a digestion year of the kind Fortinet had in 2023, and the observability bear of +5.8% a year describes a consumption slowdown where the disclosure describes the possibility of a level reset of 30-50% in a single renewal window.

What the model excludes

No acquisitions in any scenario, for the reasons above. No convertible-note or capped-call marks, because they run through other income and move with PANW's own share price; a non-cash charge of roughly $200m-$270m is already determined for Q4 FY2026. No goodwill impairment, on a base where goodwill and intangibles of $29,185m exceed book equity. And no price-volume decomposition below the three sub-lines where a unit exists: appliance unit shipments, average selling prices, like-for-like pricing and a quantified backlog are all undisclosed, and the end-customer count was last given in FY2017.

Forecast incremental margins in the base case are −26.1% in FY2026, 14.1% in FY2027, then 37-41% through FY2035 on the GAAP line and 39-42% on the non-GAAP line. No year in any scenario exceeds the best single year PANW has delivered on either basis. The base does run above the five-year realised 24.5% for a decade, which is the assumption to watch: it holds because the annuity and SASE books renew at low incremental cost, and it fails if the sales-and-marketing ratio stops improving. The FY2026 figure of −26.1% is not an artefact — GAAP operating income declines from $1,242.9m to about $661m on $2.2bn of additional revenue, because acquired-intangible amortisation goes from $166.3m to about $640m and share-based compensation from $1,295m to about $1,947m in the same year, and FY2027 stays low because amortisation steps again to $1,078m.

The modelled non-GAAP operating income adds back only share-based compensation and acquired-intangible amortisation, where PANW also excludes acquisition costs, restructuring, litigation and the convertible marks and applies a long-term tax rate, which is why the modelled FY2026 margin of 28.4% is about 70 basis points below the guided 28.9-29.2%. And FY2029 has ten revenue contributors and FY2030 six, against 38 for FY2028, so the outer consensus years are thin.

The free cash flow line is where the two disagree, and the mechanism is the customer float. Working back from consensus free cash flow to the working-capital contribution it requires, holding capital expenditure at 2.6% of revenue, gives 0.83x-0.91x per dollar of revenue growth in FY2028, 0.90x-1.02x in FY2029 and 1.17x-1.33x in FY2030, against PANW's realised 0.74x, 1.07x and 0.70x in FY2023-FY2025 and the base case's 0.58x, 0.52x and 0.48x. Consensus holds the float contribution at roughly the rate PANW has realised; the base case takes 40-45% off it, and that single assumption accounts for most of the FY2029 free cash flow gap of $799m.

18. Risks

Ranked by expected effect on operating profit or equity value over the next twelve months, which combines the sized exposure with the probability the mechanism operates inside that window.

R1. Expectations into the 2026-09-01 print, against a multiple linked to AI capital spending. Mechanism: PANW has beaten consensus revenue in fourteen of the fifteen quarters in the reaction series and consensus non-GAAP EPS in fourteen, and the next-session reaction has been negative in six of the last nine while the size of the beat compressed from 14-34% in FY2023 to 4-10% now. Beating is no longer sufficient. Exposure: the stock returned 91.1% over fiscal 2026 and closed the year at 80.5x one-year-forward consensus EPS against 47.0x a year earlier, then rose a further 12.0% to 2026-08-28. Drawdown precedents are −30.5% in seven sessions (February 2024), −26.8% (February to April 2025) and −36.0% (October 2025 to February 2026). What moved the stock most recently was not PANW: the 12.83% gain on 2026-08-27 came on an unconfirmed acquisition report. Leading indicator: the five-session run-up into the print against the next-session reaction. A beat met with a decline for a third consecutive quarter confirms the multiple is setting the return.

R2. AI data-centre hardware demand reversing, with the CEO naming the reversal. Mechanism: Q3 FY2026 product revenue was $594m, 19.8% of revenue, up 31%, part from AI data-centre inspection demand and part from passing component price increases through. Arora on 2026-06-02: "you'll tell me before I can tell you when you see when data center growth starts to taper off or plateau, this thing is going to come to roost." Exposure: product revenue annualises near $2.4bn on the Q3 run-rate, and the pass-through component reverses faster than the demand component because pricing resets at the next negotiation. Fortinet's Q3 2023 billings miss after a pandemic-era firewall pull-forward became channel digestion is the peer precedent for the same mechanism; PANW itself declined 8.06% on 2023-08-04, the session after Fortinet's print, without reporting anything of its own. Leading indicator: product revenue growth against hyperscaler capital-spending guidance, and the product share of total revenue. It was 19.5% of FY2025 revenue and 19.8% in Q3 FY2026, so the mix has barely moved despite 31% product growth; a product share above roughly 21% would show the hardware surge running ahead of the recurring base.

R3. The memory shortage compressing product gross margin. Mechanism: the disclosure escalated across two quarters, from no memory reference anywhere in the FY2025 10-K or the Q1 FY2026 10-Q, to "supply chain disruptions, such as a memory or other component shortage" in Q2, to "there is currently a global shortage of memory-related components" in Q3, with a named consequence: "constraints on the availability of memory-related components, which may lead to delays in the production and delivery of certain of our products and increased costs." Exposure: each point of product gross margin is worth roughly $24m of annual gross profit at the current run-rate. Product gross margin has already compressed from 77.8% in Q3 FY2025 to 71.9% in Q3 FY2026, and the 10-Q names hardware margin separately from purchase accounting. PANW has "no volume purchase contracts with any of our component suppliers," Flex is the sole named assembler with a convenience-termination right, and $246m of manufacturing commitments is about seven months of product cost of revenue, so PANW buys largely on spot terms into the shortage. Leading indicator: product gross margin by quarter, and the inventory excess-and-obsolete charge, which runs in the opposite direction if a shortage reverses into over-ordering.

R4. Goodwill and intangibles exceed shareholders' equity. Mechanism: six acquisitions since August 2024 rebuilt the balance sheet around purchase accounting. Goodwill went from $4,567m to $21,902m and net intangibles from $763m to $7,283m in nine months, so the two are 63.1% of total assets and $1,517m more than total stockholders' equity. The largest single identified intangible is $3,500m of platform renewals amortised over 12 to 14 years, which suppresses GAAP earnings into the late 2030s and is the line most exposed to a re-estimate if identity renewal rates disappoint. Exposure: $21,902m of goodwill against FY2025 GAAP operating income of $1,242.9m, so any write-down is measured in years of operating profit. Recognition would be late and large: one reporting unit means goodwill is tested against the whole company, so weakness in one platform is offset by strength in another until the aggregate breaks. Leading indicator: the fiscal-2027 segment disclosure and whether it creates separate reporting units; identity and observability ARR growth against the assumptions implied by a 12-to-14-year renewals life. Impairment is non-cash, so what it would change is covenant headroom on any future debt and the credibility of further stock-funded deals.

R5. Share-based compensation and share issuance. Mechanism: two dilution channels operate at once. Share-based compensation was $684m in Q3 FY2026, 22.8% of revenue, of which $177m was acceleration on the CyberArk and Koi closings; excluding it the quarter was 16.9% against 14.2% a year earlier. Unvested awards not yet recognised were $3.6bn at 2026-04-30, amortising over 2.6 years. Separately, shares outstanding went from 660m at 2025-01-31 to 813m at 2026-04-30, up 23.2% in five quarters, and Q4 FY2026 is guided at 830-840m fully diluted. Exposure: share-based compensation is the largest single reason Q3 FY2026 was a GAAP loss. Leading indicator: share-based compensation as a percentage of revenue by quarter against management's stated path from 22.8% back toward roughly 14% by late fiscal 2027, observable each quarter without waiting for the outcome.

R6. Further large stock-funded acquisitions, which the market is now paying for. Mechanism: PANW has closed six acquisitions since August 2024, and reporting on 2026-08-27 stated that Arora held talks with Okta between late 2024 and early 2025 that stalled on price, approached Datadog in spring 2025, and is now pursuing Cribl at roughly $200m of ARR and a ~$3.5bn valuation and ClickHouse at above $250m of ARR and a ~$15bn private mark, about 17x and 60x ARR [web]. A ClickHouse-scale transaction funded in stock at the 2026-08-28 price would issue roughly 40m shares on top of the 112m already issued for CyberArk, adding goodwill to a base that already exceeds book equity. Exposure: the behavioural part is the risk. The shares rose 12.83% on the day the pursuit was reported, six months after a $21bn deal produced a GAAP operating loss and negative tangible book equity, so the reward function makes further deals more likely. Integration capacity is the binding constraint and is thinly funded: the workforce optimisation plan for the combined entity is estimated at $59m in total, $12m paid by 2026-04-30, on an acquisition that added roughly 4,166 employees. Leading indicator: headcount and share-based compensation per employee against the 12-to-18-month convergence commitment; any 8-K announcing a transaction above roughly $5bn before CyberArk's integration is complete.

R7. Observability revenue concentrated on a single frontier AI lab. Mechanism: two figures from the same prepared remarks on 2026-06-02 size it. "Our observability ARR surpassed $300 million this quarter, nearly doubling since our acquisition announcement last autumn," and "In Q3, we surpassed $200 million in ARR with a leading frontier AI lab that relies on us for observability across its most demanding training and inference clusters." Both are "over" figures, so the ratio is a range and PANW does not split the $200m between observability and other platforms. Exposure: $200m is 2.5% of the $8.13bn NGS ARR, and the exposure is to AI training capital spending and to that lab's own funding, which correlates with R1 and R2. No single end customer exceeded 10% of total revenue in FY2023, FY2024 or FY2025, so the concentration is within the platform. Leading indicator: observability ARR growth once the named customer's migration completes, which management already flagged for the following quarter.

R8. Channel concentration, and a disclosed decline that is mostly a threshold effect. Mechanism: the disclosed aggregate covers only distributors individually above 10% of revenue, so it moves when a name crosses the threshold independent of any change in behaviour. The count dropped from three to two only in the nine-month period containing CyberArk from 2026-02-11, and identity revenue does not flow through the same distributors.

Period Distributors ≥10% Aggregate % of revenue % of gross receivables
FY2023 three 49% 37%
FY2024 four 59% 31%
FY2025 three 44.2% 44.8%
6M FY2026 three 42% 46%
9M FY2026 two 31% 29%

Top-three concentration at nine months is bounded between 31.0% and 41.0% of revenue against 42.0% for the same three names at six months [estimate: two distributors at 31% of $8,070m is $2,502m; the third was above 10% at six months and below 10% at nine, so between $0m and $807m]. The disclosed move from 44.2% to 31% overstates the de-concentration by as much as ten points. Exposure: two distributors were 29% of gross accounts receivable at 2026-04-30, so a distributor failure is a credit event on roughly $830m of gross receivables plus an immediate fulfilment gap. Leading indicator: the count of distributors above 10% in each 10-Q read together with the aggregate. A count that falls while the aggregate holds is arithmetic; a count that holds while the aggregate falls is real de-concentration.

R9. A defective product or content update disabling customer networks. Mechanism: PANW's firewalls are deployed inline in customer traffic and its Cortex and Koi agents are installed on endpoints, and both receive continuous content updates. The FY2024 10-K added a sentence absent from FY2023 and earlier: defects "may cause our products or subscriptions to become temporarily unavailable… or temporarily interrupt end-customers' networking traffic." The count of the token "vulnerabilit" in the 10-K went from 10 in FY2023 to 19 in FY2024 and 18 in FY2025. Three PAN-OS vulnerabilities are on the public record: CVE-2024-3400, a GlobalProtect command injection at CVSS 10.0 exploited from 2024-03-26 with roughly 22,500 internet-exposed devices assessed as vulnerable; CVE-2024-0012, an authentication bypass at CVSS 9.3 disclosed in the FY2025 10-K; and CVE-2026-0257, advised 2026-05-13, exploited from 2026-05-17 and added to the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-05-29 [web]. Exposure: CrowdStrike's 2024-07-19 content update crashed Windows hosts worldwide and its share price declined about 45% over the following 18 days; the direct customer-commitment cost was later quantified at roughly $60m of net new ARR and subscription revenue, and the multiple compression was not. PANW's own worst single session was −28.4% on a guidance change alone. CrowdStrike's event hit endpoints; an availability event affecting inline firewalls at almost all of the Fortune 100 would interrupt network traffic itself. Leading indicator: CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities entries for PAN-OS, and whether the FY2026 10-K reinstates a named vulnerability example.

R10. The headline growth metrics widen with every acquisition. Mechanism: billings was defined net of acquired deferred revenue and could not be widened; NGS ARR and remaining performance obligations both expand by acquisition and by definitional scope, and PANW's own definition says so. At 2026-04-30, $1.63bn of the $8.13bn NGS ARR came from CyberArk and Chronosphere, and reported growth was more than double organic on both metrics: NGS ARR +60% against +28%, RPO +36% against +22%. Exposure: this is a measurement risk. It matters because the headline metrics will keep flattering the growth rate for as long as PANW keeps acquiring, which R6 says it intends to. Leading indicator: the organic figures, which management currently volunteers on the call and does not disclose in the filings, and which it has said it will stop giving.

R11. Israel and regional hostilities. Mechanism: Israeli long-lived assets were $162.1m at 2025-07-31 against $141.1m a year earlier, 22.1% of the total and second only to the United States, while the US share declined. CyberArk is an Israeli company and added roughly 4,166 employees, so the post-close share is higher and is not yet disclosed. The Q3 FY2026 10-Q changed "the hostilities in Israel and the surrounding region" to "the hostilities in Israel, Iran and the surrounding region." Exposure: the real exposure is engineering continuity for the identity platform. Leading indicator: the FY2026 10-K's country split of long-lived assets, which shows the post-CyberArk Israel share for the first time.

R12. Fixed cloud commitments against consumption-priced revenue. Mechanism: PANW's cloud-delivered services are hosted on third-party infrastructure under non-cancelable minimums, while the revenue they support is consumption- and seat-priced and reprices annually. Exposure: $8,092m of cloud commitments, of which $6.4bn falls in FY2029 and beyond against revenue that does not exist yet, and subscription and support gross margin has already declined from 73.4% in FY2024 to 72.5% in FY2025 to 66.5% in Q3 FY2026. Leading indicator: subscription and support gross margin excluding intangible amortisation, and the year-one tranche of the commitment schedule relative to cloud-delivered revenue.

Which risks arrive together

Two clusters share drivers, so a bad quarter would arrive as a whole cluster.

The AI capital-spending cycle turns (R1, R2, R3, R6, R7). Hyperscaler and frontier-lab spending plateaus. Product revenue growth reverses, as Arora said it would. The memory shortage unwinds, which relieves cost but leaves inventory bought at peak prices, producing excess-and-obsolete charges in the same direction FY2025 already saw. The frontier AI lab that supplies a third to two-thirds of observability ARR slows or renegotiates. The multiple compresses from 80.5x and the acquisition speculation the market rewarded on 2026-08-27 is repriced at the same time. Every element is downstream of one variable, and the October 2025 to February 2026 episode was −36.0% without a demand reversal.

Growth bought with stock (R4, R5, R6). Goodwill and intangibles already exceed book equity, share-based compensation is 22.8% of revenue with $3.6bn unvested, and management is reportedly pursuing targets at up to 60x ARR. A further stock-funded deal deepens all three at once, and if the first cluster arrives the currency loses value, which either stops the acquisition programme or forces cash and debt funding, which PANW has not used at scale.

The overlap is R6: serial acquisition is the mechanism that converts a cyclical demand problem into a balance-sheet problem.

19. Source disclosure

Archives and databases. Ten 10-Ks covering FY2016 to FY2025 and six 10-Qs through the quarter ended 2026-04-30, with both raw and cleaned text; 24 quarterly earnings releases from Q4 FY2020 to Q3 FY2026; 40 earnings and presentation transcripts from Q4 FY2016 to Q3 FY2026, including the Citi and UBS conference appearances of September and December 2025 and the CyberArk merger call of 2025-07-30; fifteen investor and earnings decks spanning 2013-03-21 to 2026-06-02, 1,174 rendered slides; eight DEF 14A proxy statements from 2018-10-22 to 2025-11-07 and the 8-K of 2025-12-11 with the annual-meeting voting results; extracted 10-K section files for FY2016 to FY2025, including the risk-factor sections used for the year-over-year diffs; XBRL structured financials for FY2011 to FY2025 annual and quarterly; a Daloopa extraction of 8,927 values across 49 periods; and a live Bloomberg terminal pulled 2026-08-29 against the 2026-08-28 close for prices back to 2015-07-01, annual and quarterly fundamentals, the earnings-announcement history, daily one-year and two-year blended-forward consensus, per-fiscal-year BEst, the analyst recommendation and target file, and the comparable-company table.

Peer filings read directly: Fortinet, Check Point, Cisco, Zscaler, CrowdStrike, Cloudflare, SentinelOne, Datadog, Dynatrace, Elastic, Microsoft, Okta, SailPoint, and CyberArk's 20-F filings for FY2023 and FY2024 plus its 6-K filings for the third and fourth calendar quarters of 2025. CyberArk's ticker was delisted at the close, so its filings had to be pulled by CIK; the fourth-quarter 6-K required exhibit-level recovery.

Data built from those sources. A ten-year annual financial series and a twelve-quarter series, both reconciled line by line against the filings and against a Bloomberg pull; a reference class of 104 software, infrastructure-software and cybersecurity issuers from 1998 to 2026, 1,728 company-years with a computable forward growth rate, used for the base rates in Section 14; a driver-based operating model from FY2026 to FY2035 across three scenarios; the comparable-company table; and eleven derived market series covering daily prices, forward consensus, valuation history, fiscal and calendar returns, quarterly reactions, pre-print consensus, drawdowns, largest daily moves and the forward view. Dated copies of the price, multiple and comparable series were archived so the as-of record survives.

Gaps and failures.

  • No sell-side research covers this company in the local digest: 376 reports, none matching PANW or "Palo Alto." The sell-side view therefore falls through to Bloomberg consensus, and the bear arguments in Sections 8 and 18 are reconstructed from analyst questions on the archived calls, from the price-reaction record and from the company's own risk-factor changes. A real short thesis may contain arguments not covered here.
  • The 8-K of 2026-08-20 (Ex-10.1, an Executive Change in Control and Severance Policy, plus a bylaw amendment) was not read, so Section 10's severance and change-in-control terms predate it by nine days, and the parsed proxy's severance field is empty for 2023 through 2025.
  • The CyberArk merger agreement and the 2026-02-11 closing exhibits were not read, so Section 11 reports the announced-versus-booked price gap without the exchange-ratio mechanics that produced it.
  • Four of the six acquisitions in the FY2026 ledger — Chronosphere, Protect AI, Koi and Portkey — have no pre-deal financial history of any kind behind $4,563m of nine-month acquisition cash.
  • CyberArk has no audited annual report for 2025 and never will: its last 20-F covers 2024 and 2025 exists only in quarterly 6-K releases, so $21.1bn of purchase consideration and the identity segment's standalone record are underwritten off unaudited quarterly filings.
  • Two 8-K exhibits in the local earnings store were the wrong exhibit for fiscal Q4 2025 and fiscal Q1 2026, and both releases were re-pulled from EDGAR and archived.
  • Two web citations could not be re-fetched: the Google Cloud blog announcing a Leaders placement in the 2025 SIEM Magic Quadrant returns 404, and the CyberArk press release stating Venafi's ARR at close redirects. Both are noted where they are used.
  • The DuckDB research lake holds no rows for PANW in its financial-facts table, so all financial series come from the archived filings and the XBRL extractions.

Estimates. Thirty-one figures are tagged [estimate: method], and each states its inputs and its bounds. Eleven are residuals from a disclosed total: the platform revenue split, Network Security revenue, Cortex ARR and its non-XSIAM residual, cloud-security ARR, the identity stub, the privileged-access share of CyberArk ARR, PANW's share of measured network security, the firewall-plus-SASE market and the Splunk security book. Four apply the company's own published formula to disclosed balances: FY2025 billings, FY2025 Q4 non-GAAP operating income, the implied Q4 FY2026 margin and organic share-based compensation. Two are bounded arithmetic on a one-sided disclosure: top-three distributor concentration and the memory share of the bill of materials. And two are instrument arithmetic on the assumed convertible notes: the uncovered conversion cost and the fourth-quarter mark.

Corrections worth stating. Five figures that circulate elsewhere are wrong or unsourceable and are not used here. CyberArk's last GAAP operating profit was calendar 2020, not 2019, on its own SEC-tagged operating income, so the unprofitable run is five years. PANW's FY2024 non-GAAP operating-margin expansion was 320 basis points; the 340-basis-point figure that appears alongside it is the Q4 FY2025 quarterly expansion. CrowdStrike's press releases contain no Next-Gen SIEM, cloud-security or identity ARR figure, so the module-level comparisons at $585m, $600m and $695m have no primary source and the last verifiable figure is above $430m at 2025-07-31. A Dell'Oro top-four firewall share of 68% at an all-time high does not appear on the page it is attributed to, which reports the 29% / 15% / 15% split and nothing about the top four. And the drawdown and largest-move tables count calendar days, not trading sessions: the February 2024 decline of 30.5% took seven trading sessions, and the CyberArk announcement decline spanned three.

20. What is still not known, and what to watch

Named gaps

  1. The public-sector and federal vertical is not sized anywhere. Management named a federal contract that "didn't materialize at the pace and at the spending levels we had expected" as one cause of the February 2024 guidance cut, the session in which the equity lost 28.4%. No revenue figure, growth rate or share of Americas revenue exists for it in any filing or call, so the vertical that produced the largest single-session decline in the company's history cannot be sized.
  2. Unit 42's revenue is undisclosed, assumed here at $200-400m. That assumption alone moves the Network Security residual to $7.0-7.6bn on the FY2025 basis, and services gross margin is structurally below subscription, so Network Security's gross margin and its comparison with peers are unverified by the amount of that mix.
  3. Channel conflict between the NextWave partners and PANW's own services is untested. PANW had more than 8,500 channel partners at 2025-07-31 including managed security service providers, and it sells Unit 42 managed detection and response and Cortex directly into the same managed-service work those partners resell. PANW does not quantify the overlap.
  4. Customer composition by industry is not disclosed beyond "almost all of the Fortune 100" and "a majority of the Global 2000." End-market concentration is the exposure that moved the profit and loss statement in FY2024, and PANW gives no figures for it.
  5. The international position is not sized as a growth driver. PANW earns 67% of revenue in the Americas against Fortinet's 40% and Check Point's 42%, and trails Fortinet on EMEA revenue by 38%. The $2.9bn gap to the FY2030 ambition could be closed by international share as easily as by acquisition, with different capital consequences.
  6. Sales capacity is not measurable. PANW does not disclose sales-representative counts on quota, sales productivity, customer acquisition cost or payback, while the fiscal 2030 target needs roughly 101 net platformizations a quarter for seventeen quarters and the base case takes cash sales and marketing from 29.4% of revenue to 26.4%.
  7. Company-wide net retention is not disclosed. The 120% figure applies only to the roughly 2,280 platformized accounts, a cohort defined by having already consolidated, against a base of more than 65,000 firewall customers. That makes it a survivor statistic.
  8. The capitalised contract-cost balance and its amortisation period are not disclosed. Deferred sales commissions matter because a FY2017 policy change already restated three years of operating losses, and as the mix shifts from lengthening enterprise agreements toward the shorter acquired books — identity remaining performance obligations to ARR at 1.19x against a consolidated ratio near 1.6x, and Chronosphere's coverage under one year — the amortisation schedule compresses. Neither direction is quantified.
  9. Whether regulation drives demand is untested. NIS2, DORA, PCI-DSS, CIRCIA, the SEC cyber-disclosure rules and cyber-insurance underwriting could each be driving part of the appliance demand, so that line is labelled cyclical on a refresh clock while EMEA, 21% of revenue, grew 32% in the April 2026 quarter.
  10. Whether Fortinet matched the April 2026 10% hardware price increase is unknown. The increase is credited with one to three points of the roughly 40% Q3 FY2026 bookings growth, and Fortinet is winning the refresh on volume, price and margin at once. If Fortinet did not match, the increase is share given away.
  11. The frontier AI lab's exposure to in-sourcing its own telemetry is unquantified. Chronosphere is usage-priced, so revenue falls whenever that customer optimises telemetry volume independent of any competitive loss.
  12. No full quarter of the combined company has been reported. Q3 FY2026 holds only about 2.6 months of CyberArk and roughly one quarter of Chronosphere, so the identity revenue share, the combined gross margin, the purchase-accounting deferred-revenue haircut and the assumed sales-and-marketing convergence all depend on a stub period.
  13. The ten-year financial series begins at FY2016, so PANW's fastest growth years and its first deceleration, fiscal 2012 to fiscal 2015, fall outside it, and the closest analogue to the current deceleration is the company's own early history.

Appendix A — Investor-presentation insights and key slides

Fifteen decks span 2013-03-21 to 2026-06-02, 1,174 rendered slides. Most headline figures were also spoken at the same event. What the decks add is the material that lives only in chart labels and footnotes: full grids where the transcript gives one value, metric definitions, and series that can be assembled across decks but were never assembled by management.

  • The attach model priced, in 2013 (§1). Each cloud-delivered subscription listed at 20% of appliance list price per year and support at about 16%, with support attach near 100% and more than 1.5 subscriptions shipped per appliance in fiscal Q2 2013. At 2.9 subscriptions by fiscal Q4 2017 the annual recurring services value approached 74% of appliance list price. PANW has never restated that relationship for the software and SASE form factors [deck: Financial Analyst Day 2013-03-21, slide 169].
  • Renewal rates and contract duration, disclosed for four years and then dropped (§1, §3). Renewals above 90% on subscriptions and about 100% on support, unchanged FY2014 through FY2017. Contract duration moved 1.8 years (fiscal Q4 2013) to 1.9 to 2.1 and then to about 3.0 years by FY2017, at which point short-term deferred revenue covered about 45% of the next year's consensus revenue [deck: Investor Day 2017-09-27, slides 129, 155].
  • The refresh distribution (§1). Appliance lifespan is a distribution centred between four and seven years, with about 65% of the 2009 device population refreshed by FY2016, generally onto larger boxes with larger attached subscriptions. The 2015 transcript had described the same cycle as "typically on a 4- to 5-year cycle" [deck: Investor Day 2016-04-04, slides 130-131].
  • Lifetime value by cohort, and why the series ended (§3). Nine cohorts published for four consecutive years: the 2009 cohort of about 300 customers reached 17.5x its initial order by FY2017, while the 2017 cohort of about 8,500 started at 1.3x like every other. Management's install-base upside figure of more than $8bn applied the 300-customer 2009 multiple to roughly 28,000 later customers. The disclosure ended after FY2017 and never resumed, so the durability of the land-and-expand claim across the much larger cohorts acquired since has never been shown [deck: Investor Day 2017-09-27, slide 113].
  • How the sales force is paid (§5, §10). Most compensation is earned on product plus the first year of subscription and support; multi-year is commissioned at a much lower rate; renewals go to inside sales with limited compensation for the general force. The design pays for new placement, which is consistent with contract duration staying near 1.9 years through FY2015 and with the later shift toward multi-year and deferred payment terms being a finance-led change [deck: Investor Day 2016-04-04, slide 100].
  • The account-coverage ceiling (§4). About 50 global accounts, 2,000 major, 20,000 named and more than 150,000 commercial, each on a different touch model, so the high-touch tiers total roughly 2,050 accounts [deck: Financial Analyst Day 2015-03-30, slide 90].
  • Per-vendor revenue per customer (§4). PANW $41.3k against Check Point $10.3k, Cisco security $8.6k and Fortinet $4.6k in FY2017; the transcript gave only the 5.6x aggregate. The same deck shows network security appliance share moving from 3.4% in Q2 CY2012 to 14.0% in Q2 CY2017, past Check Point at 12.6% and Fortinet at 10.6% and still behind Cisco at 15.9% [deck: Investor Day 2017-09-27, slides 149, 153].
  • The acquisition playbook and its own benchmark (§11). Acquired teams run their own plays for nine months; from nine to 24 months the core sales force is leveraged, targeting a 30-40% improvement over the target's standalone plan; beyond 24 months the target is a 100% improvement and accretion. That is the framework CyberArk is being run against [deck: Analyst Meeting 2019-09-04, slide 75].
  • Where the cash comes from (§10, §13). Collections in a fiscal year on deferred-payment deals signed in a prior fiscal year supplied about 30% of FY2024 adjusted free cash flow, about 40% of FY2025 and a guided 50% of FY2026. Half of guided FY2026 free cash flow is therefore not a function of FY2026 selling, and the balance of future collections has to keep growing for the margin to hold [deck: Q4 FY2025 Earnings 2025-08-18, slide 21].
  • The 2:1 replacement claim, against the pool it was drawn from (§6). The 2021 analyst day asserted that SASE adoption drives 2:1 hardware replacement value. The FY2024 deck shows the combined firewall-as-a-platform billings pool decelerating from 28% to 26% to 17% growth as the software share rose from 41% to 67% [deck: Analyst Day 2021-09-13, slide 31; Q4 FY2024 Earnings 2024-08-19, slide 8].
  • The addressable market restated at nearly every investor day (§6). $13.4bn (2013, IDC) → $19.5bn (2014) → $22.1bn (2016) → $24.0bn (2017) → $72.6bn (2019, Gartner) → $110bn (2021) → $181bn for 2025 and $257bn for 2028 (2025). The 2019 restatement tripled the market in two years, changed the source from IDC to Gartner, and included an internally estimated "future security automation" category of $25.2bn, so roughly a third of the 2022 figure was a company estimate [deck: Analyst Meeting 2019-09-04, slides 60, 62].
  • The platformization definition, which lives only in a footnote (§6, §9). An active enterprise licence agreement or more than $1m of SASE ARR for network security; more than $1m of ARR for cloud security; an active XSIAM contract or more than $100k of QRadar SIEM ARR with Cortex XDR or XSOAR for security operations; more than $500k for identity; more than $500k for observability. Counts are taken within the 5,000 largest customers at up to five each, so the metric is capped at 25,000 and cannot register growth among the roughly 65,000 customers outside the top 5,000 [deck: Q3 FY2026 Earnings 2026-06-02, slide 6 footnotes].
  • The target scorecard across three target sets (§9, §14). The FY2016 model set in 2013 targeted 22-25% non-GAAP operating margin, reached in FY2019; the sales-and-marketing target was loosened twice, by a cumulative 5 points, while actual spend stayed between 43% and 47% of revenue. The FY2022 targets set in 2019 were beaten on billings and revenue and missed on margin at 19.0% against 21-22%. The FY2024 targets set in 2021 landed within $30m on revenue and 30% above on ARR [deck: Financial Analyst Day 2013-03-21, slide 175; Analyst Meeting 2019-09-04, slides 79, 83; Analyst Day 2021-09-13, slides 66, 86].
  • The CyberArk case, quantified (§11). 88% of attacks involve stolen credentials; CyberArk served about 8m privileged-access users against more than 1bn potential identity users; machine identities outnumber human identities by about 80 to 1. The same deck states the dilution plainly: accretive to revenue growth and gross margin immediately post-close, accretive to free cash flow per share only in FY2028 [deck: CyberArk Acquisition Investor Presentation 2025-07-30, slides 9, 11, 17].

Appendix C — External data sources

Six external datasets are available for a company of this type. None is pulled. All six are assembled by web mosaic, which means partial coverage assembled from several public pages, and each entry says what would have to be reframed for an enterprise network-security vendor.

Search-interest trends (Google Trends). Relative search interest for the company and its named products over time, and against named peers on a common query basis, published weekly as an index from 0 to 100. It would inform Section 6's growth attribution and Section 4's share discussion by giving an independent mindshare series for Prisma Access, Cortex XSIAM, Cortex Cloud and Idira against Zscaler, Netskope, Wiz, Splunk and Datadog. That would check PANW's product-level share claims against something outside its own ARR disclosures. The index is relative, not absolute, so it is a directional demand and mindshare proxy and not a units or revenue series. Transfers cleanly to this company. Not pulled.

Hiring and headcount signals (job postings, LinkedIn, layoff trackers). Open-role counts by function, separating sales and go-to-market from engineering, the total posting trend, and any headcount or restructuring action, monthly. This series would test the sales-capacity constraint behind the fiscal 2030 platformization target: Section 17's base case requires roughly 101 net platformizations a quarter for seventeen quarters while cash sales and marketing declines from 29.4% of revenue to 26.4%, and PANW does not disclose sales-representative counts on quota or sales productivity. It would also track the CyberArk integration against the $59m workforce optimisation plan, which is Section 18's R6. Pairs with the disclosed headcount series in Section 13. Transfers cleanly. Not pulled.

Service reliability and outage incidents (status pages, Downdetector, post-mortems). Frequency, duration and stated root cause of incidents over time, classified as self-inflicted or third-party, on an event cadence. It would inform Section 18's R9, where the mechanism is a defective content update disabling inline customer traffic and the sole quantified precedent available is a peer's. PANW's status-page history and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities entries for PAN-OS would give a frequency base rate where the dossier currently has three named vulnerabilities and one peer analogue. Partial mosaic, not comprehensive. Not pulled.

Developer-ecosystem adoption (package downloads, GitHub activity, developer surveys). Download trends for a vendor's software development kit or command-line tools, repository momentum, and developer-survey usage, weekly. The transfer to PANW is imperfect, because its products are appliances, cloud-delivered subscriptions and security-operations platforms bought by security teams. Where it would apply is Section 2's coverage of the container firewall, the Terraform and infrastructure-as-code security lines inside Cortex Cloud, and the Chronosphere and Prometheus ecosystem, which is developer-adopted and where Grafana's open-source base is the named low-end alternative. Would need a PANW-specific reframe around those three. Partial mosaic. Not pulled.

Web technology adoption share (W3Techs, BuiltWith, HTTP Archive). A vendor's share of public or top-ranked websites running its product, monthly, as external proof of share against named peers. Written around web-infrastructure providers and content delivery networks, so it maps only partially onto a vendor selling firewalls, SASE and security-operations platforms; the PANW surface it reaches is Prisma Access as a reverse proxy for customer traffic. It would inform Section 4's SASE share discussion, where the current evidence is management's ARR growth against a Dell'Oro market rate and no independent unit series exists. Weak transfer, and of no use unless the Prisma Access footprint is separately identifiable. Partial mosaic. Not pulled.

Internet traffic and usage telemetry (Cloudflare Radar, Similarweb). Third-party or vendor-published telemetry on internet and application traffic, bot and AI-crawler share, and product usage, monthly.
